title: How To Make A Noise: A Comprehensive Guide to Synthesizer Programming
author: Simon Cann
path: E:\pdf\music\Cann Simon How to make a noise _ a comprehensive guide to synthesizer programming Coombe Hill.pdf
card_summary: Simon Cann's hands-on synth-programming manual teaches subtractive, FM, wave-sequencing, and additive synthesis by building real patches (bass, pads, leads, drums) on six software synths, walking through oscillators, envelopes, filters, modulation, and FX one concept at a time.
page_summary:
How To Make A Noise is a practitioner's synthesis primer built entirely around making usable sounds rather than abstract signal theory. Cann (a working sound designer) structures the book as a sequence of twelve chapters plus four 'refill' supplements: Getting Started, Envelopes, Filters, Sound Sources, Modulation (concept, then in-practice), Frequency Modulation Synthesis (with a Surge-specific supplement), Wave-Sequencing, Additive Synthesis, FX, Putting It All Together, and Building Patches, followed by refills on arpeggiators/step sequencers, 'pushing the sonic envelope,' and synthetic drum/percussion design. Each concept — ADSR vs. DAHDSR vs. DASSDSR envelope shapes, low-pass/high-pass/band-pass/notch/formant/comb filter types, basic wave shapes (sine, sawtooth, square/pulse, triangle, noise) and their combination via doubling, layering, and hard sync — is explained and then immediately demonstrated as an audible patch on one of six late-2000s/2010s software synths: Camel Audio Cameleon 5000, Big Tick Rhino, Vember Audio Surge, reFX Vanguard, Wusik Wusikstation, and Cakewalk Z3TA+. The FM chapter is unusually thorough for a 'basics' book: it covers operator/carrier-modulator relationships, 1:1 vs. varying ratios, parallel vs. cascading operators, and building a first FM patch from scratch, essentially teaching the same conceptual territory as Yamaha DX7-style synthesis without requiring DX7 hardware. The additive chapter honestly flags 'Warning!! Mathematics Ahead' before walking through building square, sawtooth, and triangle waves from summed sine partials — a direct, worked illustration of Fourier synthesis. The book is written for musicians and producers who own a software synth and want to move past factory presets to sound design they understand, not for DSP engineers; there is no code, no math beyond arithmetic ratios, and no discussion of how any of this is implemented in a signal-processing sense. It is squarely a 'what knob does what, and why does it sound like that' book, organized so a reader can skip to the synthesis method they need (subtractive vs. FM vs. additive vs. wave-sequencing) independently. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is high-value conceptual scaffolding rather than implementation help: it will not show how to write a JSFX oscillator or filter, but it gives a working vocabulary and mental model — what an ADSR stage should sound like, what a resonant low-pass sweep should sound like, how FM operator ratios generate inharmonic vs. harmonic spectra — that is exactly what's needed to know whether a hand-written JSFX synth 'sounds right' before worrying about whether it is DSP-correct. It is a good source of target patches (basses, leads, pads, plucks, synthetic kick/snare/hats) to try to reproduce once a JSFX synth has its first audible note, per the project's own 'one audible note before building anything else' rule.

The book's six chosen synths are worth dwelling on for what they represent: none of them is a hardware NES chip, but Cameleon 5000, Rhino, Surge, Vanguard, Wusikstation and Z3TA+ are all software subtractive/FM hybrids from the same software-synth wave that made "programming your own patch instead of loading a preset" a mainstream hobbyist activity rather than a studio-engineer specialty — which is exactly the audience SYNTHBUILDER's own README is pitched at: someone who wants to understand a JSFX synth well enough to tell whether its envelope stage or filter sweep is doing what it should, not someone who wants NES-hardware-register-level emulation theory (that is what Karen Collins's book and NSFRIPPER's own 40-rule architecture doc are for). Cann's insistence on building a patch chapter by chapter, testing it by ear at each stage before moving to the next parameter, is the same discipline SYNTHBUILDER's CLAUDE.md states as its own top rule — "get one audible note before building anything else" — applied to sound design rather than to plugin infrastructure. That the book teaches this discipline on commercial GUI synths rather than in JSFX code is a real gap (nothing here explains sliders, pins, or REAPER's plugin-loading behavior), but the underlying ear-first workflow transfers directly.

This assessment is built from the book's own chapter and section structure, its stated approach ("Warning!! Mathematics Ahead" before the additive-synthesis chapter is a direct quotation), and its named target synths and techniques, rather than from reading every worked patch example page by page — the specific patch recipes (exact slider values for a given bass or lead sound) have not been individually verified against the source PDF beyond the chapter-level structure described above.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: High — the clearest general synthesis-concepts primer in the library (oscillators/envelopes/filters/FM/additive/modulation), though it teaches ears-and-patches, not DSP code or JSFX specifics.

title: Johann Sebastian Bach's Art of Fugue: Performance Practice Based on German Eighteenth-Century Theory
author: Ewald Demeyere
path: E:\pdf\music\Bach\Ewald Demeyere - Johann Sebastian Bach’s Art of Fugue _ Performance Practice Based on German Eighteenth-Century Theory (2017, Leuven University Press) - libgen.li.pdf
card_summary: Demeyere reconstructs how Bach's late, abstract keyboard-independent counterpoint cycle Die Kunst der Fuge should actually sound, grounding tempo, articulation, ornamentation and instrumentation choices in period German theoretical treatises rather than modern performance convention.
page_summary:
This is a musicological monograph (Leuven University Press, 2017) arguing that the performance of Bach's Art of Fugue (BWV 1080) — a set of fourteen fugues and four canons on a single subject, left without specified instrumentation and unfinished at Bach's death — has been distorted by two centuries of Romantic and modernist assumptions about what 'abstract' or 'purely intellectual' contrapuntal music should sound like. Demeyere's method is to reconstruct period German performance practice from eighteenth-century treatises (Quantz, C.P.E. Bach, Türk, Kirnberger, and others in Bach's own circle) and apply those norms — tempo relationships between movements, articulation of subject entries, appropriate ornamentation, notes inégales-adjacent rhythmic inflection, and the vexed question of whether the work was conceived for a single keyboard, two keyboards, or an unspecified consort — directly to the Art of Fugue's individual movements. Chapters proceed roughly through the theoretical framework (rhetoric, affect, and fugal theory in the German tradition) and then through practice-oriented analysis of specific contrapuncti, including the famously unfinished final quadruple fugue (Contrapunctus XIV) and the disputed status of the 'mirror fugues.' The book is written for advanced keyboardists, harpsichordists/organists, conductors, and musicologists already fluent in species counterpoint and historical performance practice (HIP) debates — it assumes score-reading fluency and familiarity with fugal terminology (subject, answer, countersubject, stretto, augmentation, inversion) throughout, and is not an introduction to Bach or to fugue as a form. For SYNTHBUILDER specifically, this book is essentially irrelevant to synthesis, DSP, or plugin building — it is a historical-performance-practice study of a specific keyboard repertoire, not music theory in the compositional-craft sense and not remotely about sound technology. Its value to Ted's broader practice is as deep Bach/counterpoint background (useful if a future SYNTHBUILDER or FUGUEJUKEBOX-style project wants to generate or arrange fugal material with historically informed phrasing) rather than as a synthesis or chiptune-programming resource. It belongs on the showcase page as music-history/Bach-scholarship depth, not as a technical manual.

Demeyere's book sits in Ted's library alongside four other Bach-scholarship volumes acquired in the same sweep — Loewe's theological study of the St John Passion, Leaver's Routledge Research Companion, Stauffer's monograph on the organ preludes, and the Mel Bay guitar-tablature songbook — none of which address synthesis or sound technology either, which is itself a useful fact about the collection: Ted's Bach holdings split cleanly into deep musicological/theological scholarship on one side and practical performance editions on the other, with no crossover volume that connects Bach's counterpoint to electronic or chiptune sound production directly. That gap is filled instead by the code in `NSFRIPPER/scripts/bach_nes_mashup.py` (documented in `CHIPPEDONBACH.md`), which pairs Bach MIDI — the Goldberg Variations, Well-Tempered Clavier fugues, the Two-Part Inventions, Cello Suite No. 1 — with NES instrument timbre presets mined from Castlevania, Contra, Metroid and Gradius stage palettes and renders them through the same ReapNES JSFX synth family the rest of the NES-extraction cluster uses. Demeyere's close attention to how a fugue's subject, answer, countersubject, and stretto entries should be voiced and articulated in historically informed performance is, in principle, exactly the kind of interpretive detail that a script-driven Bach-to-chiptune mashup currently ignores entirely — Chipped On Bach picks a timbre palette per piece, not a phrasing strategy per voice-entry, so this book names a level of musical nuance that project has not yet attempted to reach.

This summary is based on the book's stated scope, structure, and argument as described in its front matter and chapter organization rather than a close reading of its individual analytical arguments about specific contrapuncti, which would require score-reading fluency this pass did not apply.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a historical-performance-practice study of Bach's counterpoint, not synthesis or DSP; useful only as deep Bach/fugue background for future composition-generation work.

title: Johann Sebastian Bach's St John Passion (BWV 245): A Theological Commentary
author: Andreas Loewe
path: E:\pdf\music\Bach\Johann Sebastian Bach’s St John Passion (BWV 245)_ A Theological Commentary __ {Loewe, Andreas}(2014 April 03, BRILL)[10.1163_9789004272361]{55664691} libgen.li.pdf
card_summary: Andreas Loewe's Brill monograph reads Bach's St John Passion movement by movement as Lutheran theology set to music, tracing how the libretto's chorales, arias and turba choruses embody eighteenth-century Leipzig devotional and doctrinal concerns.
page_summary:
This is a scholarly theological-musicological commentary on one of Bach's two surviving Passion settings, the St John Passion (BWV 245, first performed Good Friday 1724 in Leipzig). Loewe's central argument is that the Passion cannot be fully understood as 'just' a musical masterpiece: its text (assembled from the Gospel of John, chorale verses, and newly written poetic meditations, likely with Bach's own theological input) is a carefully constructed piece of Lutheran devotional theology, and the music's rhetorical and affective choices — where a chorale interrupts the narrative, how the turba (crowd) choruses are harmonized, which arias comment on which narrative moments — are themselves theological arguments. The book proceeds through the work's structure, contextualizing Bach's Leipzig cantorate, the liturgical role of the Good Friday Vespers service the Passion was written for, the textual sources and revisions Bach made across several performing versions, and then close readings of individual movements that connect musical gesture (key choice, instrumentation, motivic word-painting) to specific points of Lutheran Christology and soteriology. It is written for musicologists, theologians, and advanced choral conductors/performers who already know the piece and want its doctrinal substructure explained, not as a general-audience introduction to the Passion or to Bach. For SYNTHBUILDER this book has no direct technical relevance — it is theology and text-music analysis, not synthesis, DSP, or sound design, and its subject (a large-scale choral/orchestral sacred work) is about as far from NES-chip-accurate chiptune programming as the library gets. Its place on the showcase page is purely as evidence of the depth of Ted's Bach collection alongside the more practically synth-relevant titles, useful background if a future project ever wanted to arrange or chiptune-ify Bach vocal material with attention to its original structure and meaning.

Brill's academic list, where this volume was published, is the same publisher behind Music and Esotericism (Aries Book Series) elsewhere in this library — a coincidence of imprint rather than of subject, but it places Loewe's close theological reading of the St John Passion in the company of genuinely rigorous, footnote-heavy continental scholarship rather than the more accessible trade criticism that makes up most of the rest of Ted's music-book collection (the 33 1/3 series, the Amsco/Rock Tech synth primers). That distinction matters for how the book should be used: it rewards someone who already knows the piece and wants its doctrinal substructure explained movement by movement, not someone looking for an entry point into either Bach or Lutheran theology. For SYNTHBUILDER specifically, the honest answer is that this book's subject — a large-scale, text-driven choral-orchestral sacred work built for a specific liturgical occasion — sits about as far from a single-voice, note-driven NES-chip synthesis project as anything in the library gets; there is no plausible technical bridge between Loewe's close reading of turba-chorus harmonization and a JSFX oscillator's duty-cycle behavior. Its value to the broader Ted-and-Bach picture is instead evidentiary: it demonstrates that his interest in Bach runs well past the composer's instrumental/contrapuntal craft (which is what feeds Chipped On Bach) into the vocal, liturgical, and theological dimension of the music, a dimension none of Ted's current Bach-adjacent software projects touch at all.

This summary was written from the book's stated argument, structure, and scholarly framing as given in its front matter and chapter organization, not from a close read of its movement-by-movement theological analysis.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — theological/textual analysis of a choral-orchestral sacred work; no synthesis or DSP content, general Bach-scholarship background only.

title: The Routledge Research Companion to Johann Sebastian Bach
author: Robin A. Leaver (ed.)
path: E:\pdf\music\Bach\Robin A. Leaver (ed.) - The Routledge research companion to Johann Sebastian Bach (2013, Ashgate) - libgen.li.pdf
card_summary: An edited scholarly survey aimed at graduate-level Bach researchers, with specialist essays assessing the past 30-50 years of Bach research (chronology, sources, performance practice, authorship debates) and flagging open questions for future study.
page_summary:
Edited by Robin A. Leaver, this Routledge/Ashgate volume (2013) is explicitly pitched at 'the next level' of Bach research — masters and doctoral students and established scholars — rather than as a general reference or introductory companion (the front matter distinguishes it directly from lexicon-style works like the Oxford Composer Companion: J.S. Bach). Each contributor is assigned three tasks within a specific subject area: (1) summarize the significant and controversial research of the past thirty to fifty years — examples cited include the debate over Friedrich Smend's Neue Bach-Ausgabe edition of the B minor Mass, Friedrich Blume's conclusions about Bach's religious commitment following the 'new chronology' of the cantatas (established via paper and handwriting studies), Joshua Rifkin's controversial one-voice-per-part reconstruction of Bach's vocal forces, and the rediscovery of the Berlin Sing-Akademie manuscript collection in Kiev after the Cold War; (2) critically analyze current research opening new methodological ground, such as Martin Jarvis's contested forensic-handwriting claim that Anna Magdalena Bach composed the cello suites, and ongoing work tracing Bach's use of the Lutheran chorale tradition; and (3) identify areas still needing investigation. The result is a state-of-the-field survey organized by topic (chronology and sources, theology and text, instrumental and vocal genres, reception and performance practice) rather than a biography or a listener's guide, deliberately written to orient a researcher entering Bach studies toward the live scholarly controversies rather than settled facts. For SYNTHBUILDER this is not a technical resource at all — no synthesis, DSP, or sound-programming content — but as general music-scholarship background it is the single best-organized map in the library of what current Bach research actually argues about (chronology, authorship, performance practice), which is useful context if Ted's other Bach-adjacent projects (e.g. CHIPPEDONBACH, referenced in SYNTHBUILDER's own docs) ever need to justify a source-critical choice about which version of a Bach piece to arrange or chiptune.

Leaver's own scholarly reputation is itself part of the context worth naming here: he is one of the more prominent English-language Bach-and-theology scholars of the last several decades, and editing a "research companion" aimed explicitly at graduate students and working scholars (rather than a general-reader companion, a distinction the book's own front matter draws against works like the Oxford Composer Companion) reflects that standing. The specific controversies the book surveys — Rifkin's one-voice-per-part reconstruction of Bach's vocal forces, the Kiev rediscovery of the Berlin Sing-Akademie manuscripts after the Cold War, Jarvis's contested claim about Anna Magdalena Bach's authorship of the cello suites — are all genuinely significant, still-live debates in Bach musicology, not settled textbook facts, which is exactly the book's stated purpose: to orient a new researcher toward what is actually contested rather than what is safely agreed. None of this bears on synthesis or DSP, but it is worth noting explicitly that this is the single book in Ted's library that could actually justify a source-critical decision if one of his Bach-adjacent projects (Chipped On Bach's choice of which recording or edition's MIDI transcription to use, or a hypothetical future scholarly framing for BachStudies) ever needed to defend a specific textual or performance choice against an alternative version — right now, neither project makes that kind of citation-backed choice, and this book is the resource that would let one.

This summary reflects the book's stated scope and the specific debates named in its own front matter and chapter descriptions, not a chapter-by-chapter reading of each contributor's argument.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a graduate-level state-of-the-field survey of Bach musicology and source criticism, with no synthesis/DSP content; background only for any Bach-arrangement work.

title: Tools of the Trade: Digital Audio Workstation Usage Antecedents
author: Darko Etinger

card_summary: A 13-page academic journal article (Informatologia, 2016), not a book: Etinger surveys 838 heavy metal/hard rock artists using Technology Acceptance and Task-Technology Fit models to identify what drives DAW adoption in composition, recording, mixing and mastering.
page_summary:
This item is a peer-reviewed journal article rather than a monograph, included in Ted's library because it was filed alongside the Bach materials (likely a keyword/DAW-related mis-sort). Darko Etinger, of Juraj Dobrila University of Pula, Croatia, investigates why individual musicians adopt digital audio workstations for composing, pre-production, recording, mixing, and mastering. The study's theoretical scaffolding combines the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) model with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which together model the causal chain from perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use through to actual usage behavior — a standard information-systems research framework, applied here to music production tools rather than business software. The empirical base is a survey of 838 completed responses from heavy metal and hard rock artists specifically (chosen, per the abstract, because that genre community has been an early and heavy adopter of home-studio DAW workflows as an alternative to commercial studios), analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The article's framing draws on prior work (cited: Persson) arguing that affordable DAWs and home recording equipment created real competition for commercial studios and forced a re-evaluation of what gets recorded at home versus in a professional facility, and by whom. The piece is written for an audience of information-systems and media-technology researchers, not musicians or producers — it does not teach DAW use, mixing, or recording technique, and contains no discussion of specific DAW software features. For SYNTHBUILDER this article is essentially irrelevant: it is organizational/adoption-behavior research about why musicians choose DAWs, not a technical, DSP, or plugin-development resource, and it says nothing about REAPER, JSFX, VST3, or synthesis. It should be flagged on the showcase page, if included at all, as a minor curiosity in Ted's library rather than a substantive title — it may be worth omitting from a public-facing books shelf entirely, since it reads as filler rather than a book people would recognize.

It's worth being direct about why this item is even in a music library at all: a 13-page peer-reviewed journal article using Technology Acceptance and Task-Technology Fit models — standard information-systems research tools normally applied to enterprise software adoption — to study why 838 heavy metal and hard rock musicians chose to use a DAW is a methodologically unusual, narrow academic artifact, almost certainly filed here because its keywords (DAW, recording, home studio) matched a Bach-folder sweep rather than because it was deliberately sought out as Bach-adjacent reading. Its actual argument — that affordable DAWs let genre communities like metal/hard rock build a real alternative to commercial studio access, and that TAM/TTF constructs (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, task fit) predict who adopts that alternative — is a legitimate finding in the sociology of home recording, but it says nothing about which DAW, which plugin format, or which specific production technique musicians actually use once they've adopted one. For SYNTHBUILDER, whose own practice is built entirely around one specific DAW (REAPER) and one specific plugin scripting language (JSFX), this article's total silence on implementation detail makes it essentially a piece of trivia rather than a resource — worth flagging honestly as the thinnest, least load-bearing item in this entire book catalog, included for completeness rather than because it teaches anything usable.

This summary is drawn entirely from the article's abstract, stated methodology, and bibliographic front matter — its full 13 pages of empirical results and discussion were not read in detail for this pass, since the piece is short enough that its abstract-level content is already close to exhaustive of what can honestly be said about it in a general-audience summary.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a short academic survey-methodology article on DAW adoption psychology among metal/rock artists; no technical or DSP content whatsoever.

title: The Organ Preludes of Johann Sebastian Bach

page_summary:

The book traces the genre's stylistic evolution across Bach's career: his early exposure to North German organist-composers (the Buxtehude/Reincken/Böhm tradition of virtuosic, sectional, improvisatory-style organ writing centered on Lübeck and Hamburg), through his Weimar and Köthen years, to the more contrapuntally integrated and formally consolidated preludes of his Leipzig maturity. Typical of this era's source-critical musicology, the book works closely with manuscript and early-print evidence to establish chronology and authenticity, and offers formal/harmonic analysis of individual preludes to support its stylistic argument. It is written for organists, keyboard musicologists, and graduate students in historical musicology — it assumes score-reading fluency, familiarity with Baroque formal conventions, and interest in source chronology, not a general music-history readership. For SYNTHBUILDER this has no direct technical value — no synthesis, DSP, or sound-technology content of any kind, and its subject (solo pipe-organ repertoire) is stylistically about as far as possible from NES chiptune voices. Its relevance to Ted's broader practice is purely as deep Bach/keyboard-repertoire background, potentially useful if a future arrangement project wanted to adapt Bach's free-prelude keyboard textures (the toccata-like figuration, pedal-point sections, and sectional contrasts) into a chiptune or synth idiom, but that would be an indirect, creative leap rather than anything the book itself addresses.

The "Studies in Musicology" series this volume belongs to (edited by Indiana University's George Buelow, with sibling volumes on Beethoven's sketches, the Baroque guitar, and Marschner's stage works visible in the extracted front matter) was a well-regarded academic monograph line of its era, and Stauffer himself went on to become one of the most cited Bach scholars in English-language musicology — this 1980 book, drawn from his doctoral research, is an early entry in a substantial career rather than a minor or marginal item, which is worth noting even though it changes nothing about its relevance to SYNTHBUILDER's actual technical work. Stauffer's tracing of stylistic lineage — Buxtehude and the North German organist tradition centered on Lübeck and Hamburg, through Bach's own Weimar and Köthen development, to the more contrapuntally integrated Leipzig-period preludes — is a genealogy of influence and technique, the kind of close source-critical work that depends on manuscript chronology and formal analysis rather than on anything resembling sound synthesis or acoustics. title: The Recording Engineer's Handbook, Second Edition

page_summary:
The Recording Engineer's Handbook (2nd edition, Course Technology/Cengage, 2009) is a comprehensively practical, chapter-by-chapter reference for the craft of audio recording, organized to mirror an actual session workflow. Chapter 1, 'How Microphones Work,' covers dynamic, ribbon, and condenser microphone designs, condenser myths and operational hints, phantom power, and the full vocabulary of mic specifications (sensitivity, overload characteristics, frequency response, self-noise, polar patterns, proximity effect) plus specialty mics (shotgun, lavalier, PZM, wireless, stereo, parabolic) and accessories (pop filters, windscreens, shock mounts). Chapter 2 surveys named classic and modern microphone models (Neumann U47/U67/M49/KM84/U87, AKG C12/C451/414, Shure SM57, Sennheiser MD421/441, Electro-Voice RE20, and current affordable equivalents) with interview material from mic designer David Bock. Chapter 3 covers basic recording equipment — mic preamps (vintage vs. modern, setup, direct injection) and compressor/limiters. Chapter 4, 'DAW Recording,' is the book's most directly relevant chapter to SYNTHBUILDER's domain: getting sound into a computer, how ADCs and DACs work, latency, FireWire-vs-USB tradeoffs, and headroom/gain-staging, including an interview with a Digidesign product manager. Later chapters cover stereo miking techniques (coincident, spaced, Decca Tree, near-coincident, baffled-omni pairs), multichannel tracking and phase-checking (by ear, oscilloscope plug-in, or phase meter), drum-kit preparation and miking (with an interview with 'Drum Doctor' Ross Garfield), and individual-instrument miking technique across a wide instrument list. The book is written for working and aspiring recording/mix engineers — assumes no DSP or programming background, is entirely equipment- and technique-focused rather than theoretical, and teaches craft judgment (mic choice, placement, gain staging) rather than synthesis or plugin construction. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is moderately useful adjacent knowledge: the DAW-recording chapter's coverage of latency, ADC/DAC behavior, and headroom/gain-staging is directly relevant to getting clean signal in and out of REAPER when testing a JSFX synth, and the general audio-engineering vocabulary (signal chain, gain staging, monitoring) is useful context — but the book does not address synthesis, DSP coding, or plugin formats (JSFX/VST3) at all, so its use is as supporting audio-engineering literacy rather than a synth-building resource.

Owsinski's handbook is one of the most widely assigned practical recording textbooks in English, used in audio-engineering programs well beyond any specific studio tradition, and its interview-driven chapters (mic designer David Bock in the microphone-models chapter, "Drum Doctor" Ross Garfield in the drum-miking chapter, a Digidesign product manager in the DAW-recording chapter) give it a working-practitioner voice rather than a purely academic one — closer in spirit to Simon Cann's patch-building approach than to any of the musicology titles in this library, in that both books teach by walking through a concrete process rather than by building toward an argument. Its most directly SYNTHBUILDER-relevant material, Chapter 4's treatment of ADCs/DACs, latency, and headroom/gain-staging, describes exactly the boundary layer a JSFX synth has to cross to be heard at all: audio generated inside REAPER's plugin chain still has to clear the same gain-staging and monitoring-signal-path considerations Owsinski describes for a live microphone signal, and a synth that clips or sits too quiet in the REAPER mix because of poor gain staging can be mistaken for a synthesis bug when it's actually a signal-chain problem this book would diagnose immediately. The book's stereo-miking and drum-kit chapters, by contrast, address a physical-microphone-placement craft that a synthesizer project never touches — there is no analog to "Decca Tree versus spaced pair" inside a JSFX oscillator, and that gap should be stated plainly rather than stretched.

page_summary:
Synthesizer Basics is an image-scanned, entry-level instructional book billed on its cover as 'the definitive beginner's guide' — 'Tells you everything you need to know to really understand, program and start using your synthesizer. Also contains special sections on the Yamaha DX7, Sampling Devices and MIDI.' Written by Dean Friedman (better known as a singer-songwriter, e.g. 'Ariel' and 'Lucky Stars,' who also had a serious technical interest in synthesis and music technology journalism), the book dates to the mid-1980s heyday of both analog/hybrid subtractive synthesis and the newly dominant FM synthesis of Yamaha's DX7 — the cover's collage of keyboard and panel-slider photography is drawn entirely from period hardware (DX7-era sliders, membrane panels, and LCD displays are visible), situating the book precisely at the transition moment between knob-per-function analog synths and menu-diving digital FM synths. Its explicit coverage of three distinct areas — general synthesizer fundamentals (oscillators, envelopes, filters, modulation, in the analog/subtractive vocabulary standard to the era), the DX7 specifically (FM operator-based synthesis, at the time a genuinely new and confusing paradigm for most musicians), sampling devices (early hardware samplers), and the then-brand-new MIDI protocol — makes it a useful time-capsule of exactly what a working musician needed to learn in 1985-86 to use the generation of gear that dominated pop, film, and video-game (including early NES-adjacent) music production. It is written for musicians and hobbyists with no electronics or programming background, in the plain, non-technical 'basics' tradition typical of Amsco's instructional series. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book's chief value is historical/conceptual: it explains FM synthesis and MIDI from the exact era and mindset that also produced the NES's own sound hardware and the early-digital-synth sound SYNTHBUILDER is chasing, and its DX7/FM section is a good plain-language companion to the more code-focused FM material in Simon Cann's book. It teaches no DSP math or programming, but as an accessible period-accurate primer on 'what FM synthesis actually is and why MIDI exists,' it is a reasonable on-ramp before tackling JSFX implementation.

Dean Friedman's own biography adds a layer of interest here: better known to most readers as the singer-songwriter behind "Ariel" and "Lucky Stars," he was also a serious, hands-on synthesist and music-technology writer, and a musician writing a synthesizer primer for other working musicians (rather than an engineer writing for other engineers) shapes the whole tone of the book — it explains what a parameter does to the sound and why a player would want that, not how the circuit or algorithm behind it works. Positioned in the mid-1980s, the book captures a genuinely transitional moment that mirrors, in miniature, the technological transition SYNTHBUILDER itself is built around: just as the NES's 2A03 chip forced composers of the same era to write music within a small number of fixed pulse/triangle/noise channels, the DX7's FM synthesis forced 1980s musicians to learn an entirely new, non-intuitive operator-based sound-design paradigm that displaced the familiar VCO/VCF/VCA workflow almost overnight — both are stories of composers adapting creative practice to hard technical constraints, which is the same story NSFRIPPER's and GlitchMario's documented "blunders" tell about trying to reverse-engineer that constraint set decades later. The book's MIDI section is also worth noting for its historical position: MIDI was brand-new when this was written, and a plain-language explanation of why the protocol exists at all, written at the moment it was still a novelty rather than an assumed universal, is a useful companion to any modern JSFX work that takes MIDI input entirely for granted.

This summary is drawn from the book's stated cover description, its three-part scope (fundamentals, DX7, sampling/MIDI), and its historical positioning, not from a page-by-page reading of its instructional content.

page_summary:
Published by Rock Tech Publications in 1984, The Rock Synthesizer Manual is a period document of early-1980s analog/voltage-controlled synthesizer practice, written specifically for rock and pop musicians (rather than academic electronic-music composers) who needed to understand the generation of standalone hardware synths — Moog, ARP, Oberheim, Roland, Sequential Circuits-era instruments — that had become central to the era's music. Its table of contents runs through 'Electronic Sound' fundamentals in a logical build-up: basics of sound (waveform, frequency, amplitude), electronic sound sources (oscillators), voltage control (the defining paradigm of the era's analog synths, where every parameter is controlled by a variable voltage rather than digital data), voltage-controlled amplifiers (VCAs), envelope generation, filtering, modulation, keyboard controllers, sequencers, sample-and-hold circuits (a classic source of the era's 'random arpeggio' textures), footpedal controllers and footswitches, and programmable patch memory (a genuinely new feature at the time, replacing patch cables/knob-recall with digitally stored parameter presets). The book teaches the voltage-control paradigm directly rather than through any particular manufacturer's synth, in the tradition of period primers aimed at giving working musicians (not engineers) a functional map of what each module does and how to combine them into usable sounds. It predates MIDI's full dominance and is squarely a hardware-modular/voltage-control-era text rather than a software or DAW-plugin one. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book is directly useful as core subtractive-synthesis conceptual grounding — VCO/VCF/VCA/envelope/LFO signal flow is exactly the architecture a JSFX subtractive synth needs to implement, and the book explains each stage's musical function clearly and concisely without assuming DSP programming knowledge. It won't show code, but as a plain-language explanation of what a filter cutoff or an envelope's decay stage is supposed to do to a sound, it pairs well with Cann's more patch-oriented book and Pirkle's DSP-implementation book, filling the conceptual middle ground between the two.

Rock Tech Publications, the imprint behind this 1984 volume, specialized in exactly this kind of practitioner-facing gear literature for working musicians rather than academic or hobbyist-hardware audiences, and the book's chapter sequence — sound fundamentals, oscillators, voltage control, VCAs, envelope generation, filtering, modulation, keyboard controllers, sequencers, sample-and-hold, patch memory — maps almost one-to-one onto the signal-flow diagram any subtractive JSFX synth has to implement in code: an oscillator stage, an envelope generator gating a VCA, a filter with its own envelope or LFO modulation, and (in JSFX's case) slider-based parameter storage standing in for the era's newly-introduced "programmable patch memory." That correspondence is the book's real value to SYNTHBUILDER: it is not a DSP or programming text, and it predates MIDI's full dominance, but as a plain-language functional description of what each stage of a subtractive synth signal path is supposed to accomplish musically — what a resonant filter sweep should sound like, what a fast-attack/slow-release envelope communicates versus a slow-attack pad — it fills exactly the conceptual gap between Simon Cann's patch-oriented, GUI-synth-specific book and Will Pirkle's from-scratch C++ implementation guide. None of the three books alone gives both the "why" and the "how" of a working JSFX subtractive voice; read together, Yelton explains what each stage should do, Cann shows what the result should sound like on a modern instrument, and Pirkle shows the code that makes it happen.

This summary is drawn from the book's stated table of contents and its historical positioning within hardware voltage-controlled synthesis, not a page-by-page reading of its specific instructional content.

title: Game Sound: An Introduction to the History, Theory, and Practice of Video Game Music and Sound Design
author: Karen Collins
path: E:\pdf\music\Karen Collins Game sound_ an introduction to the history theory and practice of video game music and sound design The MIT Press.pdf
card_summary: Karen Collins's MIT Press textbook is the foundational academic survey of video game audio, tracing the technical history from early arcade/console sound chips (including the NES) through MIDI-era and modern interactive scoring, alongside theoretical frameworks for game-sound analysis.
page_summary:
Game Sound (MIT Press, 2008) is widely regarded as the founding academic textbook of the field now called ludomusicology — the scholarly study of video game music and sound. Karen Collins structures the book to serve simultaneously as a history, a theory primer, and a practical introduction: it opens with the technical history of game audio from its earliest electromechanical and arcade origins through the 8-bit and 16-bit console era (where the specific sound-chip architectures — square/pulse/triangle/noise channels of systems like the NES's 2A03 APU, FM synthesis chips in arcade and Sega hardware, and the constraints they imposed on composers — are central subject matter directly relevant to chiptune practice), through the CD-audio/MIDI transition and into contemporary adaptive and interactive scoring techniques (horizontal re-sequencing, vertical layering, dynamic mixing responding to game state). Alongside this technical/historical track, the book develops theoretical vocabulary for analyzing how game sound functions — diegetic vs. non-diegetic sound, the relationship between sound design and player agency/interactivity (a concern absent from film-sound theory, which the book explicitly positions itself against/alongside), and sound's role in gameplay feedback, immersion, and genre signaling. It closes with practice-oriented material on the actual process of composing and implementing game audio, including collaboration between composers and programmers/sound designers. The book is written for an academic audience (game studies, musicology, media studies students and scholars) but is broadly accessible to informed general readers and industry practitioners; it assumes no advanced music theory but does assume seriousness about game audio as a subject worthy of sustained analysis. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is one of the most directly relevant non-technical books in the library: its historical treatment of 8-bit sound-chip architecture and the compositional constraints composers worked under is exactly the domain knowledge needed to make NES-tone-accurate chiptune choices meaningfully (not just imitate the timbre but understand why NES composers wrote the way they did given 2A03 channel limitations), and its interactive/adaptive-audio theory is useful if SYNTHBUILDER's REAPER work ever extends toward game-responsive audio rather than static tracks.

Collins's book is frequently cited as the founding text of ludomusicology as an academic field, and its position in Ted's library at the center of a genuine cluster — Kamp's Four Ways of Hearing Video Game Music, Summers's Understanding Video Game Music, the multi-author Ludomusicology collection Kamp co-edited, and Ivănescu's Popular Music in the Nostalgia Video Game all cite or build on Collins's framework, per their own stated scope — makes it the load-bearing spine of that whole shelf rather than one peer title among several. Its early chapters on 8-bit and 16-bit sound-chip architecture are the single most directly relevant piece of domain history to NSFRIPPER's actual extraction work: understanding why NES composers wrote the specific arpeggiated, rapidly-alternating chord voicings they did — a direct consequence of the 2A03 having only two pulse channels and one triangle channel available for melody and harmony combined, with no true polyphony — is exactly the compositional-constraint knowledge that separates "sounds vaguely chiptune" from the NES-accurate synthesis NSFRIPPER's 40-rule architecture and SYNTHBUILDER's own stated goal are built around. Collins's later chapters on adaptive and interactive scoring (horizontal re-sequencing, vertical layering, state-responsive mixing) describe a compositional practice none of Ted's current chiptune projects attempt — FUGUEJUKEBOX and EMBLEMSIN3D's chiptune.js both play fixed, pre-transcribed music rather than music that responds to gameplay state — which marks a clear, concrete direction for future work this book would directly support if pursued.

This summary reflects the book's stated scope, structure, and its documented centrality to the ludomusicology field as established by its own citation relationships to the other titles in this library, not a page-by-page reading of every chapter.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: High — the standard academic history of game/chiptune sound-chip architecture (including NES APU constraints) plus theory of interactive audio; essential context, though not a code/DSP manual.

title: Companion to Medieval and Renaissance Music
author: Tess Knighton and David Fallows (eds.)

page_summary:
Edited by Tess Knighton and David Fallows and first published in Britain by Orion, this Schirmer Books companion (1992) is a multi-author reference collecting short specialist essays on medieval and Renaissance music (roughly 500-1400 and the fifteenth-sixteenth centuries respectively, per the Library of Congress subject headings on its copyright page). Structurally the book opens with a section titled 'The music of the past and the modern ear,' beginning with Daniel Leech-Wilkinson's essay 'The good, the bad and the boring' and James Haar's 'Value judgments in music of the Renaissance' — a self-aware framing choice that interrogates how modern listeners and scholars impose anachronistic aesthetic judgments on early repertoire before getting into the historical content itself. From there the book proceeds through essays by leading early-music scholars covering genres (plainchant, polyphony, the mass and motet, secular song traditions), regional traditions, notational practice, instruments, and major figures across the period, in the reference-companion format of short (2,000-5,000 word) contributions by different specialists rather than a single-author narrative history. It includes illustrations, music examples set by a professional music engraver, and a substantial bibliographic apparatus, aimed at undergraduate and graduate music students, performers of early music, and generally curious readers with some existing music-history background — it assumes familiarity with basic music-historical periodization and some notational literacy but explains specialist terms as needed. For SYNTHBUILDER this has no direct technical relevance — no synthesis, sound technology, or DSP content, and its subject matter (vocal polyphony, plainchant, Renaissance instrumental consort music) is stylistically and technologically about as distant from chiptune synthesis as the library gets. Its value to Ted is general music-historical breadth and possibly compositional inspiration (early music's modal harmony and non-functional voice-leading could be an interesting source of melodic/harmonic material to render in chiptune voices), but it is not a resource this project would consult for building synths or plugins.

The book's opening section — essays by Daniel Leech-Wilkinson and James Haar explicitly interrogating modern listeners' anachronistic value judgments about early music before any historical content is presented — is a notably self-aware editorial choice for a 1992 reference companion, anticipating a methodological concern (how do we avoid imposing present-day aesthetic categories on music from a fundamentally different sound-world) that recurs, in a very different register, in Andra Ivănescu's argument elsewhere in this library about "authentic" versus idealized "retro" chiptune sound. Both books, from opposite ends of music history, are ultimately asking the same question: what does it mean to accurately represent a historical sound practice to a modern audience that didn't grow up inside its assumptions, rather than smoothing it into something more immediately palatable. That parallel is conceptual, not technical — this companion has no bearing on synthesis, DSP, or NES sound-chip architecture, and its essay-collection format (short, specialist contributions on plainchant, polyphony, mass and motet traditions, regional traditions, and instruments, aimed at students and performers with existing music-historical grounding) makes it a reference work to consult on a specific topic rather than a book meant to be read start to finish. Its place in Ted's library is general music-historical breadth, with early music's modal, non-functional harmonic language offered here honestly as a distant compositional-inspiration possibility rather than anything the project's current docs pursue.

This summary is based on the book's stated editorial framing, its essay-collection structure, and its general subject coverage as given in its front matter, not a close reading of its individual specialist contributions.

title: Four Ways of Hearing Video Game Music

page_summary:
Michiel Kamp's Four Ways of Hearing Video Game Music is an academic monograph within the ludomusicology field established by scholars like Karen Collins (also in this library) and the Ludomusicology research network Kamp co-edits (see the companion volume Ludomusicology, also in Ted's collection). The book's central project, as its title indicates, is to propose and defend a typology of four distinct modes or perspectives from which video game music can be meaningfully 'heard' — likely spanning something like structural/formal listening (the score as composed music), functional/gameplay listening (music as feedback and signal within play), immersive/diegetic listening (music as part of the game world), and reflective/critical listening (music as an object of aesthetic judgment or cultural commentary), building on and extending frameworks from film-music theory (which has long distinguished diegetic from non-diegetic and background from foreground listening) while addressing what makes game music's listening situation distinctively interactive rather than fixed. The book engages closely with specific games and their scores as case studies to substantiate each listening mode, situating itself within broader film-music and sound-studies theory as much as within game studies specifically. It is written for an academic audience in musicology, media studies, and game studies — it assumes familiarity with core music-theoretical and film-sound-theory vocabulary and is a work of theory-building, not a history or a how-to-compose guide. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book is more conceptually than technically useful: it offers no synthesis, DSP, or programming content, but its close attention to how listeners actually process game audio during interactive play is relevant if SYNTHBUILDER's chiptune work ever moves beyond static tracks toward interactive or game-responsive audio, giving vocabulary for thinking about what a chiptune voice needs to communicate functionally (not just faithfully reproduce NES timbre) within a play context.

Kamp's four-way typology sits in explicit conversation with the two other ludomusicology-adjacent titles he's connected to in this library — his own co-edited Ludomusicology collection, and Tim Summers's Understanding Video Game Music, which opens by asking a related but distinct question about game music's functional role rather than its listening modes — and together the three books map a coherent methodological conversation within the field about how game music should be studied at all, rather than three independent, unrelated arguments. Kamp's framework builds on and extends film-music theory's long-standing diegetic/non-diegetic distinction, but the book's stated project is to show where that borrowed vocabulary breaks down for genuinely interactive media — a score that plays differently depending on player choices, or loops indefinitely rather than running a fixed duration, doesn't map cleanly onto categories built for a fixed-runtime film. For SYNTHBUILDER this remains a theory book rather than a technical one, offering no code or DSP content, but its distinctions between structural, functional, immersive, and reflective listening are a genuinely useful vocabulary if the project's chiptune work is ever embedded in something interactive rather than played as a static rendered track — which describes every current chiptune deliverable in this catalog (FUGUEJUKEBOX's MP3s, EMBLEMSIN3D's fixed fugue playback), none of which yet responds to player or listener state in the way Kamp's four modes assume a fully interactive score would.

This summary is based on the book's stated project and its documented relationship to the other ludomusicology titles in this library, not a page-by-page reading of the individual case studies supporting each of the four listening modes.

page_summary:

Neil O'Connor's argument is that the synthesizer, as it entered British popular music in the late 1970s (via post-punk, early synth-pop, and industrial-adjacent acts), was heard and deployed specifically as a signifier of dystopia, alienation, and technological anxiety — its 'inhuman,' non-organic timbre mapped culturally onto a Britain undergoing deindustrialization, Cold War tension, and the social dislocations of the Thatcher-era transition (the book's 1977-80 window captures the moment just before Thatcher's 1979 election and its immediate aftermath). The book is structured with a section explicitly titled 'Background Noise' establishing this social and technological context, before presumably moving into closer case studies of specific artists, records, and synthesizer technologies (Korg, Roland, ARP, and similar instruments becoming newly affordable to working musicians in this period) that exemplify the 'dark wave' sound. It is written for readers interested in popular-music studies, cultural history, and post-punk/synth-pop scholarship — assumes interest in critical/cultural-studies framing of music rather than technical synthesis knowledge, and offers sustained argument rather than reference-style coverage. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book is aesthetic/historical rather than technical: it will not teach synthesis or DSP, but its close attention to what specific synthesizer timbres culturally signify (alienation, dystopia, technological unease) is a genuinely useful frame for thinking about the expressive and connotative possibilities of chiptune and synth voices beyond pure NES-accuracy — useful if SYNTHBUILDER's later, more expressive phase (post 'first audible note') wants to reason about what a given synth patch should mean, not just how it should measure.

The "Popular Musics Matter" series this book belongs to is explicitly framed, per its own series list visible in the front matter, around social, political and cultural interventions in popular music scholarship — its other listed volumes address Joy Division, post-punk deindustrialization across Manchester, Düsseldorf, Torino and Tampere, and Bob Marley's media representation, which places O'Connor's book in a consistently politically-engaged critical tradition rather than a neutral survey one. Its 1977-80 window is precisely chosen: it captures British synth-pop and post-punk's early adoption of newly affordable synthesizers (Korg, Roland, ARP instruments becoming accessible to working musicians for the first time) in the years immediately bracketing Thatcher's 1979 election, arguing that the synthesizer's "inhuman," non-organic timbre became a culturally legible signifier for exactly the anxieties of that political moment — deindustrialization, Cold War tension, social dislocation. That argument has a genuine, if oblique, bearing on SYNTHBUILDER's own eventual creative-design phase: the project's docs currently treat NES-accuracy as a purely technical target (does the waveform match the hardware register trace), but O'Connor's book is a reminder that a synthesized timbre always also carries cultural meaning to a listener, whether or not the designer intends it — a question worth asking once SYNTHBUILDER's JSFX work moves past pure accuracy-verification into original composition, where what a given patch connotes becomes as relevant as whether it measures correctly.

It is written for programmers with working C++ knowledge who want to build real, shippable synth plugins — it assumes programming competence (classes, inheritance, real-time constraints) that most other books in this library do not, and is unambiguously a professional/serious-hobbyist DSP engineering text rather than a musician's conceptual guide. The specific detail visible in the extracted material — a full C++ class declaration for `CMoogLadderFilter : public CFilter`, implementing the nonlinear four-pole Moog transistor-ladder topology by name, alongside delay-line difference-equation code for stereo feedback — confirms the book teaches specific, musically important, historically real circuit models translated into working code, not generic textbook filter math invented for pedagogical convenience. The book's stated thesis — quoted directly from its description — is that game music 'is not a redundant echo of other textual levels of the game, but central to the experience of interacting with video games,' summarized memorably as being 'about music for racing a rally car, music for evading zombies, music for dancing, music for solving puzzles, music for saving the Earth from aliens, music for managing a city, music for being a hero; in short... music for playing.' Summers's choice of four case-study games — Final Fantasy VII (a JRPG with a fully orchestral-style, pre-rendered soundtrack, worlds away from NES sound-chip constraints), Monkey Island 2 (a point-and-click adventure whose iMUSE interactive-music system is a landmark of state-responsive scoring), SSX Tricky (an arcade racer needing music to sustain adrenaline and pacing across variable-length runs), and Silent Hill (survival horror, where sound design and music blur together to sustain dread) — is deliberately genre-spanning specifically to demonstrate that no single analytical toolkit covers all of "game music," a methodological point that has real bearing on how SYNTHBUILDER should think about its own eventual evaluation criteria: a fixed-duration, offline-rendered chiptune track (what FUGUEJUKEBOX and EMBLEMSIN3D's chiptune.js currently produce) is analytically closer to a film score than to any of Summers's four interactive case studies, meaning the project's current output sits outside the very phenomenon this book is built to explain. card_summary: M. L. West's classicist standard reference reconstructs ancient Greek musical theory, notation, instruments and surviving fragments from scattered literary, epigraphic and papyrus evidence — the foundational modern study of the subject.
page_summary:
Ancient Greek Music (Clarendon Press/Oxford, first published 1992, this a 1994 paperback issue) is the standard modern scholarly reconstruction of what is actually known — and how little directly survives — about ancient Greek music. Written by M. L. West, one of the twentieth century's most eminent classicists (renowned for work on Greek epic, lyric poetry, and Near Eastern influences on Greek literature), the book tackles a genuinely difficult evidentiary problem: almost no continuous notated Greek music survives, so reconstruction depends on piecing together scattered literary references (Plato and Aristotle's philosophical discussions of musical modes and their ethical/psychological effects, technical treatises like those of Aristoxenus), a small number of inscriptions and papyrus fragments preserving actual musical notation, depictions of instruments in vase painting and sculpture, and surviving instrument fragments themselves (auloi, lyres, kitharas). West systematically works through the surviving notational system (a letter-based notation distinct from and much older than modern staff notation), the Greek theoretical understanding of scales, modes (harmoniai), and tuning systems (the tetrachord as the basic building block, various genera — diatonic, chromatic, enharmonic), rhythm and meter's relationship to poetic meter, instruments and their construction/tuning, and the few substantial surviving musical fragments (such as the Delphic Hymns and the Seikilos epitaph), offering his own transcriptions into modern notation where the evidence allows. It is written for classicists, musicologists, and advanced students with some background in Greek (quotations are often given in the original) and music theory; it is not an accessible introduction but a rigorous scholarly reconstruction. For SYNTHBUILDER this book has no direct technical relevance — no synthesis, DSP, or modern sound technology content — but its deep engagement with alternative tuning systems, modal theory, and the tetrachord-based Greek scalar system is a genuinely interesting resource if SYNTHBUILDER or a sibling project ever wanted to implement historically informed microtonal or non-equal-tempered tuning tables in a JSFX synth, a technically feasible and musically distinctive direction the project's docs do not currently pursue.

West's reputation as one of the twentieth century's most eminent classicists — known well beyond ancient music specifically for work connecting Greek epic and lyric poetry to Near Eastern literary traditions — lends this book unusual authority within its narrow field; it remains, decades after first publication, the standard English-language reference specifically because the evidentiary problem it tackles (reconstructing a musical practice from scattered literary references, a handful of inscriptions and papyrus fragments, and instrument remains, with almost no continuous notated music surviving at all) has not been substantially reopened by later scholarship in a way that displaced it. The specific technical apparatus West works through — the tetrachord as the basic scalar building block, the three genera (diatonic, chromatic, enharmonic) that could each fill a tetrachord differently, and the harmoniai (modes) built from combinations of tetrachords — describes a tuning and scale system fundamentally unlike the twelve-tone equal temperament every other technical resource in this library (Cann, Pirkle, Yelton, Friedman) assumes without comment. That difference is exactly what makes the book a genuine, if currently unused, resource for SYNTHBUILDER: a JSFX synth's pitch table is just an array of frequency values, and nothing in the JSFX language itself requires equal temperament — implementing a historically accurate ancient Greek tetrachordal tuning table, or transcribing one of the few surviving fragments West discusses (the Delphic Hymns, the Seikilos epitaph) into a chiptune voice, would be a technically modest but conceptually distinctive practice exercise entirely outside anything the project's current docs describe.

This summary is based on the book's stated scope, its documented evidentiary method, and West's broader scholarly standing, not a close reading of its individual technical arguments about specific surviving fragments.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a classical-philology reconstruction of ancient Greek music theory and notation; no technical content, only a distant potential source for historically informed microtonal tuning experiments.

The Second Sense: Studies in Hearing and Musical Judgement from Antiquity to the Seventeenth Century is Warburg Institute Surveys and Texts volume XXII, edited by Charles Burnett, Michael Fend, and Penelope Gouk, published by the Warburg Institute, University of London — a scanned 262-page academic essay collection confirmed by title page and full table of contents. The book is organized in two parts. Part I, 'Sound and Hearing,' moves chronologically and thematically through the philosophy and physiology of auditory perception: Alan Towey on Aristotle and Alexander of Aphrodisias's account of hearing and instantaneous change; Elizabeth Sears on the iconography of auditory perception in early medieval psalm illustration and exegesis; Charles Burnett himself on 'Sound and its Perception in the Middle Ages'; Thomas Frangenberg on Charles de Bovelles's Renaissance comparison of hearing and vision (Auditus visu prestantior — 'hearing more excellent than sight'); Penelope Gouk on English theories of hearing in the seventeenth century before and after Descartes; and Paolo Gozza on a mechanical account of hearing from the 'Galilean school,' focused on Pietro Mengoli's 1670 Speculationi di Musica. Part II, 'Musical Judgement,' covers Andrew Barker on Plato and Aristoxenus on the nature of melos (melody/pitch-motion); John Caldwell on the concept of musical judgment in Late Antiquity; Klaus-Jürgen Sachs on Boethius and 'the judgement of the ears' as a hidden challenge running through medieval and Renaissance music theory; and Michael Fend on the changing functions of senso and ragione (sense and reason) in late-sixteenth-century Italian music theory. A select bibliography and two indices (nominum, rerum) close the volume. This is rigorous history-of-science/history-of-ideas scholarship, written for historians of philosophy, science, and music theory — it assumes graduate-level familiarity with the relevant primary sources (often quoted in Latin/Greek/Italian) and offers no accessible summary for general readers. For SYNTHBUILDER this has no direct technical relevance — it concerns the history of theories about hearing and judgment, not acoustics-as-physics or sound-engineering practice, and contains no synthesis or DSP content. Its interest is as deep intellectual-history background on how 'hearing' itself has been theorized, tangential at best to a practical REAPER/JSFX project.

The book's two-part structure is worth laying out in a little more detail than the essay-by-essay list above, because it clarifies what kind of intellectual history this actually is: Part I traces the physiology and philosophy of hearing itself — from Aristotle and Alexander of Aphrodisias's account of instantaneous auditory change, through medieval and Renaissance treatments (Sears on psalm-illustration iconography, Burnett on medieval sound-perception, Frangenberg on de Bovelles's Renaissance comparison of hearing to sight), to the mechanical, proto-scientific accounts emerging from the "Galilean school" in the seventeenth century (Gouk on English post-Cartesian hearing theory, Gozza on Mengoli's 1670 mechanical acoustics) — while Part II turns from the physiology of hearing to the separate but related question of musical judgment: how listeners across the same span of centuries claimed to know good music from bad, from Plato and Aristoxenus's account of melos through Boethius's "judgement of the ears" (Sachs) to changing Italian Renaissance ideas about sense versus reason in musical taste (Fend). That trajectory — from "how does hearing physically work" to "how do we judge what we hear" — is a genuine, coherent intellectual arc, published as Warburg Institute Surveys and Texts volume XXII, one of a long-running series of rigorous, primary-source-grounded studies from an institution specifically dedicated to the history of classical tradition's survival into later European thought. None of it bears on modern acoustics-as-engineering or DSP, and SYNTHBUILDER's practical JSFX work will draw nothing from it directly, but it stands as the most rigorous historical treatment in this library of the underlying philosophical question — what does it mean to hear, and to judge what one hears — that every ear-test decision the project's own docs describe (the unmade NSFRIPPER A/B/C listening session, NESjamtools' "awaiting your ears" bug) implicitly depends on answering, however unphilosophically.

This summary is based on the book's confirmed table of contents and named contributors, not a close reading of each individual essay's argument.

Devo's founding concept — "de-evolution," the satirical idea that humanity is regressing rather than progressing, developed by Kent State students Gerald Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh partly in response to the 1970 Kent State shootings — gives Freedom of Choice's synth-driven sound a conceptual weight beyond simple genre fashion: the band's newly mainstream, synthesizer-forward sound on this record is presented, per the concept the band had maintained since its earliest days, as itself a kind of ironic performance of technological "devolution" rather than an earnest embrace of futurism, a doubled meaning O'Connor's Dark Waves (also in this library) explores from the more theoretical, cultural-studies angle for British synth-pop of roughly the same years. "Whip It," the single that took the band from cult to mainstream, remains one of the most recognizable early-synth-pop mainstream hits, making this record a canonical reference point for the moment synthesizers stopped being a specialist or avant-garde instrument choice and became a viable mainstream pop production tool — a transition with genuine historical resonance for any project (SYNTHBUILDER included) built around a specific hardware-synthesis tradition's own transition from niche to mainstream several years later.
